narration: A giant isopod is only giant beside the woodlice under a garden stone.
Most deep-sea creatures are not big. Gigantism appears in particular groups, mainly cold-blooded crustaceans and molluscs such as giant isopods, giant amphipods and giant squid.
For those groups, the sharpest single clue came in 1999, when a study in Nature linked the largest amphipod sizes to how much oxygen the water holds.
That settles less than it sounds. It shows where the giants tend to occur.
On its own, it does not show why they grow, or whether depth has anything to do with it.
Why are deep sea creatures so big?

Start with the part the popular image leaves out. Watch footage from a remotely operated vehicle descending through the deep water column, and you will see that most of what drifts past its lights is small: jellies, shrimp, copepods, worms, and the larvae of animals that live somewhere else.
On the seafloor, much of the life is buried in the mud, and a lot of it is too small to see without a microscope.
The giants in the thumbnails are real, but they are scattered. Animals you could hold on a fingertip outnumber them many times over.
So the honest version of the question is narrower. Why do some deep-sea animals grow much larger than their shallow-water relatives?
Biologists call that pattern deep-sea gigantism, or sometimes abyssal gigantism. You will find the term in explainers published by NOAA Ocean Exploration and Smithsonian Ocean.
The word relatives is doing the work. A giant isopod is only giant next to the small isopods of coastlines and gardens, the woodlice you may have found under a stone.
It is always a comparison within a group, not across the whole ocean.
The examples that come up again and again have something in common.

The giant isopod, Bathynomus giganteus, scavenges on the deep seafloor. Alicella gigantea is a giant amphipod, a relative of the small sandhoppers on a beach, and it has been hauled up in baited traps from great depth.
Sea spiders are usually tiny, but in cold water they reach the size of a dinner plate.
The giant squid, Architeuthis, is among the longest invertebrates known. Fish, as a group, do not show the same consistent pattern.
Many of the most common deep-sea fish, such as bristlemouths and lanternfish, are small.
Look at what the giants share. They are ectotherms, animals whose body temperature follows the water around them.
Most are crustaceans or molluscs. The same groups also produce giants in the shallow, cold seas around Antarctica, where great depth plays no part.
That overlap is the first real clue in this story. It suggests that depth itself may not be the cause.
Cold may be. On this reading, depth matters mostly because the deep is where the cold water is.
We talk about the ocean like it's a known thing because it's on every map.
Most of what's under the surface is barely documented. We're living on a planet we haven't finished looking at.
Biologists have long observed a pattern called Bergmann's rule: within related groups, larger forms tend to be found in colder places.
It was first described for warm-blooded animals. A related pattern holds for ectotherms, and it is usually called the temperature-size rule.
Raise the same species in colder water in a laboratory and, very often, it grows more slowly but reaches maturity at a larger body size.
In many of these animals, the cells themselves also tend to be larger at low temperature.
Below the surface layers, the deep sea is cold, close to freezing in many places, and it stays that way all year.
No warm season speeds things up. So the chain runs like this: cold water, slower growth, later maturity, larger adult body.
The way this mechanism is known is what gives it weight. You do not have to infer it from a few odd specimens.
You can test it in tanks, changing one variable at a time and holding the rest steady, and the result repeats across many species.
Temperature alone does not explain why size should have an upper limit.
Oxygen might. As an animal grows, its volume rises faster than its surface.
Larger animals therefore have less surface relative to their volume, and getting oxygen to every cell becomes harder.
Cold water helps in two separate ways. First, cold water holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water does.
Second, cold slows the animal's metabolism, so each cell needs less. Supply goes up while demand goes down.
In 1999, Gauthier Chapelle and Lloyd Peck, the latter of the British Antarctic Survey, published the amphipod oxygen study in Nature.
Amphipods were a good choice. They live almost everywhere, in warm water and in cold, and the largest known sizes of many species had already been recorded.
The two researchers compared those maximum sizes against the conditions where the animals lived.
Temperature on its own was not the best predictor. The amount of oxygen the water could carry was. Where oxygen was plentiful, the biggest amphipods appeared.
Why would that apply to the deep sea? Much of the ocean's deep water began as cold surface water near the poles.
That water sank and spread along the ocean floor, carrying its oxygen with it.
So a great deal of the deep sea is both cold and reasonably well oxygenated, the combination the amphipod study pointed to.
There is a useful exception. In many regions, layers at middle depths run low on oxygen, and those layers are not known for giants. That fits the idea. It does not prove it.
The second family of explanations is about food. Below the sunlit layer, nothing photosynthesises in open water.

Most deep-sea life therefore depends on what sinks from above: dead plankton, faecal pellets, flakes of drifting debris, and now and then the carcass of a fish or a whale. Food arrives rarely, and it lands in places nobody can predict.
A larger body changes the arithmetic. It stores more. And under a relationship known as Kleiber's law, bigger animals burn energy more slowly per gram of tissue than small ones do.
Put those together. Food arrives rarely, a larger body stores more, it burns energy more slowly per gram, and so a big scavenger can travel and wait.
Giant isopods kept in aquariums are known for going very long stretches without eating.
A large amphipod can cover more seafloor and reach a fallen fish before smaller competitors do.
This explanation has a weakness worth saying aloud. Scarce food can argue the other way.
Less food can just as easily mean smaller bodies. In many deep-sea groups, typical size falls with depth, while in some it rises.
Food may favour giants among mobile scavengers and favour small bodies among animals that sit in the mud and wait.
Scarce food is not a push toward large size everywhere. The same pressure produces different outcomes depending on how an animal makes its living.
There is also a quieter problem underneath all the explanations so far: how the animals were found in the first place.
Much of what is known about deep-sea giants comes from trawls dragged along the seafloor and from baited traps lowered on long lines.
A baited trap attracts mobile scavengers, which are exactly the animals the food argument predicts will be large.
A coarse net keeps big animals and lets small ones slip through the mesh.
And big, strange specimens are the ones that get described, photographed and remembered.
None of this makes the giants imaginary. A giant isopod on a laboratory bench is a giant isopod.
But the impression of a deep sea full of large animals partly reflects what the trap caught, not what lives there.
Fair comparisons need the same gear, used the same way, at the same depths, across many sites, with shallow-water relatives measured just as carefully.
Studies built like that are slow and expensive, and there are still relatively few of them.
For most of history, the largest deep-sea animals were known only from dead or dying specimens, washed ashore or brought up tangled in nets.
That limits what you can learn. You can measure a body on a deck.
You cannot see how it hunts, how fast it moves, or how much energy it spends doing so.
In 2004, Tsunemi Kubodera and a colleague took the first photographs of a live giant squid in the wild, off Japan.
In 2012, a team including Kubodera recorded the first video of a giant squid in its natural habitat.
In 2025, an expedition run by the Schmidt Ocean Institute with the Ocean Census filmed a colossal squid alive in its natural habitat for the first time, near the South Sandwich Islands.
It was a juvenile, and it was small. That is a useful correction.
Even the animal often described as the heaviest invertebrate on Earth starts life tiny.
How it becomes enormous is a question about growth in cold, dark water over a long time, and live observation can begin to answer that kind of question.
When footage of a deep-sea giant appears, watch for scale. Many remotely operated vehicles project laser dots a fixed distance apart, which lets scientists measure what is on screen.
Without a scale bar or laser dots, size on video is a guess from the frame.
Notice, too, where the animal is. Often it is at bait, or in a vehicle's lights, which is the sampling problem described earlier.
And notice what is not on screen: the small animals all around it.
Here is what this evidence does not establish. It does not show that depth itself makes animals large.
Cold, oxygen and food all change with depth, and they are hard to separate in the field.
The oxygen link is a correlation across species, strongest in amphipods, and researchers still debate how well it extends to other groups.
So whether oxygen sets the ceiling remains open. Which cause matters most probably differs from one group to another, and in many groups it has never been measured.
What is settled is narrower. Gigantism appears in particular groups, and cold water slows growth in ectotherms in ways laboratories can measure.

The deep sea is not a place where everything grows huge. It is a place where a few kinds of animal, in cold water, given time, and with food scattered far apart, can outgrow their relatives in warm, shallow seas.
The giants are real. The explanation is still being assembled, one trap, one camera and one careful comparison at a time.
